Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • 01Explain what map algebra is and how raster layers can be combined cell by cell to perform spatial analysis.
  • 02Distinguish among local, neighborhood/zonal, and global raster operations based on how much of the raster is used to calculate each output cell.
  • 03Define raster extent and raster resolution, and explain how cell size affects the amount of spatial detail represented in a raster.
  • 04Apply and interpret common raster analysis methods.
  • 05Explain what a surface is in GIS and how x, y, and z values are used to represent terrain and elevation.
  • 06Interpret basic terrain analysis concepts derived from elevation data, including slope and other surface characteristics.

Introduction to map algebra

Map algebra is the cell-by-cell combination of raster data layers. The combination entails applying a set of local and neighborhood functions, and to a lesser extent, global functions, to raster data. The concept of map algebra is based on the simple, flexible, and useful raster grid structure.

Simple operations may be applied to each grid cell. Further, raster layers may be combined through operations such as layer addition, subtraction, and multiplication.

Three types of operations

Raster operations are grouped by how much of the raster each output cell depends on:

  • LocalUse only the data in a single cell to calculate an output value.
  • Neigh.Neighborhood / Zonal operations gather input from a focal cell and surrounding cells to calculate output values at the focal cell.
  • GlobalGlobal operations may produce uniform output, or different values for each raster cell. They may return a single number, placed in every cell of the output layer.

Raster extent and spatial resolution

Raster extent: the total geographic area covered by the raster dataset. It defines the outer boundaries of the raster in space, or how much of the world the raster includes.

Raster resolution: refers to the real-world size of each pixel or cell in a raster dataset (e.g. 2 m × 2 m or 30 m × 30 m). This means each pixel represents an area on the Earth’s surface with those dimensions. For example, a 2 m × 2 m pixel represents a square that is 2 meters wide and 2 meters tall, so it covers 4 square meters on the ground.

Each pixel stores only one value for that entire area, so as cell size gets larger, more real-world variation is averaged or generalized into a single value. That is why larger cells produce less spatial detail and a coarser resolution, while smaller cells capture more detail and have a finer resolution. Finer isn’t automatically better, though — smaller cells mean much larger files, and resolution finer than the source data can’t add real detail.

Local operations

There is a broad number of local functions (or operations) that can be conveniently placed in one of four classes: mathematical functions, Boolean or logical operations, reclassification, and multilayer raster overlay.

Mathematical operations

We may generate a new data layer by applying mathematical functions on a cell-by-cell basis to input layers.

Logical (Boolean) operations

A logical operation (also known as Boolean) typically involves the comparison of a cell to a scalar value or set of values, and outputs a “true” or a “false” value. In Boolean operations, True = 1; False = 0.

  • ANDtrue only if both inputs are true
  • ORtrue if at least one input is true
  • NOTswitches true for false, and false for true. Note that null input assigns null output.

Notes:

  • •Non-zero = true
  • •Zero = false
  • •Nulls = usually return null, but some systems treat them as false

Logical operations may be provided that perform ordinal or equality comparisons, or that test if cell values are null.

Reclassification

Raster reclassification assigns output values that depend on the specific set of input values. Assignment is most often defined by a table, ranges of values, or a conditional test. It is one of the most common raster tools — used to simplify many input values into a few meaningful classes.

Raster clip and overlay

A raster clip keeps cell values inside a template or mask and assigns null outside it; a raster overlay combines multiple layers to produce a new output layer.

Neighborhood operations

Neighborhood operations most often depend on the concept of a moving window. The window is positioned on a given location over the input raster, and an operation is applied that involves the cells contained in the window. The window is then “moved” to be centered over the adjacent cell and the computation is repeated.

Moving windows are defined in part by their dimensions. For example, a 3 by 3 moving window has an edge length of three cells in the x and y directions, for a total area of nine cells.

Edge detection

The values on one side of the kernel are subtracted from the values on the other side. Large differences result in large output values, while small differences result in small output values. Edges are defined as those cells with output values larger than some threshold.

High-pass filters

Kernels that accentuate differences between adjacent cells. Useful in identifying the spikes or pits that are characteristic of “noisy” data. Cells identified as spikes or pits may then be evaluated and edited as appropriate, removing the erroneous values.

Smoothing

The mean filter both “smooths” data and increases spatial covariance in the output data set. Averaging combines nearby cells, bringing high or low values nearer the local mean. Nearby values become more similar, meaning they have a higher spatial covariance.

Zonal operations

Zonal functions apply operations based on defined regions, or zones, within an area. Typically, the zones are recorded in a data layer, with a unique identifier for each zone. A zonal summary answers questions like “what is the average elevation within each watershed?”

Cost surface

A cost surface gives the minimum cost of reaching cells in a layer from one or more source cells.

  • •Units can be money, time, etc.
  • •Distance measure is combined with a fixed cost per unit distance to calculate travel cost.
  • •If multiple source cells, the lowest cost is typically placed in the output cell.

Introduction to terrain analysis

What is a surface?

Typically, when we talk about surfaces, this involves a third elevation value (z) in addition to the x and y horizontal values. Surfaces are complex to represent since there are an infinite number of potential points to model.

Digital Elevation Models (DEM)

  • •Each cell stores the elevation value as an attribute.
  • •A surface grid considers each sample as a square cell with a constant surface value.
  • •Simple conceptual model.
  • •Data is cheap to obtain.
  • •Easy to relate to other raster data.

Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN)

A set of adjacent, non-overlapping triangles computed from irregularly spaced points, with x, y horizontal coordinates and z vertical elevations. Ideal for irregularly spaced sample points.

Point clouds

  • •LiDAR produces massive point clouds where each point has an x and y coordinate and a z value for elevation.
  • •These point clouds can be stored and analyzed in a GIS.
  • •Point clouds can be classified so that the land cover type for each point is identified.
  • •Point clouds can be rendered to create 3D visualizations.

Contour lines

Contour lines, or isolines, connect points that have the same elevation.

  • •Close lines = steep slope
  • •Uphill V = stream
  • •Downhill V or bulge = ridge
  • •Circle = hill top or basin

Poor for computer representation: no formal digital model. Must convert to raster or TIN for analysis.

Terrain analysis techniques using a DEM

Slope

Slope is a commonly used terrain variable required in many studies of hydrology, conservation, site planning, and infrastructure development. Slope is defined as the change in elevation (a rise, here axis A) with a change in horizontal position (a run, here depicted as B). Slope is often reported in degrees, between 0 and 90, although it may also be reported in percent.

Slope direction does not always point parallel to the raster rows or columns. In this example, higher elevation occurs at the lower right corner, and lower elevation occurs near the upper left. The direction of the steepest slope trends from one corner to the other and does not pass directly through the center of any cell. So how do we obtain values for the rise and run?

Aspect

Aspect is the direction of steepest slope, expressed in degrees from 0 to 360, where North = 0. Flat areas are assigned a value of −1. Uses: fire management, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and flora and fauna distribution and abundance.

Hillshade

A hillshade raster (gray) mimics the appearance of a uniform topographic surface under an illumination source. The source is placed at a designated azimuth (direction) and zenith angle (altitude). Hillshade is made for visualization — it helps us read terrain by eye, and is not usually analyzed directly.

Key takeaways

1
Raster analysis works cell by cell. We can analyze one cell at a time, compare it with nearby cells, or use information from the whole raster depending on the question we are asking.
2
Extent and resolution shape what a raster can show. Extent tells us how much area the raster covers, while resolution tells us how much detail each pixel can represent. Smaller cells show more detail; larger cells show less.
3
Different raster operations answer different questions. This week we worked with local operations like math, Boolean logic, reclassification, and overlay, as well as neighborhood operations that use a moving window.
4
Raster tools help us simplify, detect, and highlight patterns. We can identify change, smooth noisy data, summarize values within zones, or characterize terrain.
